messages.author: 26cd59ee29299001
messages.subject: Precision
parts:
Dear INLA groups,

Am doing my research with Bayesian hierarchical model. for my study I have one random factor(region) and I obtained the precision of region to be 12.71. Thus, my question is I was bit confused with its interpretation. some literature preferred to interpret standard deviation; but still I did't get what that standard deviation was exactly mean? Thank you for your professional help



With Honor Regards,


Endale

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Precision
parts:
Precision = 1 / Variance

if you rather want the posterior for the stddev, you can do as follows.
for other models you have to chose the correct hyperparameters. the
'internal' gives the posterior in the internal scale, which is
log(precision), so the change of variable becomes stdev =
sqrt(1/exp(log.precision))



> r = inla(y~1,data = data.frame(y=1:10))
> names(r$internal.marginals.hyperpar)
[1] "Log precision for the Gaussian observations"
> m.sd = inla.tmarginal(function(x) sqrt(1/exp(x)),
r$internal.marginals.hyperpar[[1]])
> inla.zmarginal(m.sd)
Mean 2.94156
Stdev 0.690075
Quantile 0.025 1.94294
Quantile 0.25 2.4522
Quantile 0.5 2.82296
Quantile 0.75 3.2955
Quantile 0.975 4.63018
> plot(inla.smarginal(m.sd), type="l", xlab = "stdev", ylab =
"posterior(stdev)")

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Precision
parts:
Hi,
Yes, virtually all numerics is safer when done closer to the “source”. Transforming the density representation is always a lossy operation (since it’s essentially a finite evaluation of a spline approximation), so it’s safer to not do a whole chain of such transformation, but instead calculate the desired quantities directly from the representation used in the construction of the inla-approximation itself.

Finn

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Precision
parts:
Agree with Finn. This also applies to computing expected values, like

> inla.emarginal(function(x) 1/x, r$marginals.hyperpar[[1]])
[1] 4.382642107
> inla.emarginal(function(x) 1/exp(x),
r$internal.marginals.hyperpar[[1]])
[1] 4.401299512

so the E(variance) is more accurate when computed from the internal....
which is log(precision).

PS: I know, E(variance) does not make so much sense, but its only an
example


With informative data, then it does not really matter, but in general,
I compute everything from '$internal.marginal...' if I need something
else than what's in the output.

H
